summary: A 1979 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols. It replaced RFC 750 and was replaced by RFC 758. It is historic.

eli5.summary: A big list saying which number means which thing in the network's rules, since replaced by a newer one.

subtitle: Updated registry of assigned numbers for network protocols in 1979

tldr.problem: Protocols and network numbers continued to be assigned; the 1978 registry (RFC 750) needed updates to remain current.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel issued an updated assigned-numbers registry covering link numbers, socket numbers, network numbers (now with 26 assignments including DIALNET and MITREK), IP versions, and protocol formats with new entries for Gateway-to-Gateway and other protocols.
tldr.outcome: The registry continued to serve as the authoritative source for protocol numbers and assignments. It was again replaced the following year by RFC 758.

today: RFC 755 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 758. The incremental registry updates documented in these RFCs evolved into the modern IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) system, which maintains similar registries today.

sections.title: Maintaining the Registry
sections.content:
RFC 755 is the 1979 update to the assigned numbers registry. Like RFC 750, it documents all numbers assigned in ARPANET and internet protocols: link numbers, socket numbers, network addresses, protocol versions, and protocol numbers. Jon Postel continued to manage assignments and maintain the registry.

This version consolidates six earlier RFCs (750, 739, 604, 503, 433, 349) into one comprehensive list, maintaining the tradition of keeping a single authoritative source as the network and its protocols evolved.
sections.eli5: The list was updated again a year later with new networks and protocols that had been added or discovered.

sections.title: Updated Assignments
sections.content:
The network numbers section grew from 22 to 26 assignments, adding DIALNET (22), MITREK Cable Network (23), BBN Local Network (24), and RSRE/PPSN (25). Socket and link assignments remained largely the same, with some additions to the protocol format identifiers (now including Gateway-to-Gateway on protocol 3, and more internet protocols).

The IP protocol numbers section expanded to include new variants tested and deployed in the late 1970s. The socket ranges and their meanings (0–63 standard, 64–127 host-specific, 128–223 reserved, 224–255 experimental) remained consistent with the 1978 version.
sections.eli5: More networks and protocols got added to the lists. The basic structure stayed the same, but the registries grew as the internet expanded.

sections.title: Periodic Updates
sections.content:
RFC 755 notes that the registry would continue to be updated periodically, with current information always available from Jon Postel. The RFC maintains the same reference format as RFC 750, citing the Protocol Handbook and other RFCs for detailed specifications.

RFC 755 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 758 in 1980, which continued the annual or biennial update cycle. This pattern of maintained, authoritative registries eventually evolved into the modern IANA system.
sections.eli5: This was just the latest version. Jon would keep updating it as more protocols got assigned numbers. The next year there would be another update.
